body:
Background and composition

After the Second World War, Britain faced increasing pressure to transfer power in India. The Indian National Congress wanted independence and a democratic constitutional arrangement. The All-India Muslim League demanded a separate Pakistan. The major challenge was to establish an agreed method of transferring power while resolving the disagreement over India's political unity.

In March 1946, the British government sent a Cabinet Mission consisting of 3 members:

  • Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Secretary of State for India.
  • Sir Stafford Cripps.
  • A. V. Alexander.

The mission held discussions with Indian political leaders and issued its principal constitutional statement on 16 May 1946.

The proposed Union of India

The Cabinet Mission did not recommend the immediate creation of 2 fully sovereign states. Instead, it proposed a Union of India embracing both British Indian provinces and princely states, with a deliberately limited central government.

Under the plan, the Union would control:

  • Foreign affairs.
  • Defence.
  • Communications.
  • Finances necessary to administer these Union subjects.

All other subjects and residuary powers were to remain with the provinces. Residuary powers are powers over subjects not specifically assigned to another level of government.

Princely states would retain powers other than those they agreed to transfer to the Union. The arrangement attempted to preserve India's political unity while limiting central authority.

The Cabinet Mission's proposed Union was much weaker than a conventional strong central government. Defence, foreign affairs and communications were the principal Union subjects; most other governmental powers were intended to remain at lower levels.

The 3 provincial sections

The mission divided British Indian provinces into 3 sections for constitution-making. These sections were commonly identified as A, B and C.

SectionProvincesGeneral characteristic
AMadras, Bombay, United Provinces, Bihar, Central Provinces and Orissa6 provinces
BPunjab, North-West Frontier Province and Sind3 provinces
CBengal and Assam2 provinces

The representatives of each section were to consider provincial constitutions and whether a group constitution should be established. Under the plan's procedure, the sections were an initial part of constitution-making, while provinces were given a later opportunity to opt out of groups by a decision of the provincial legislature after the first general election under the new constitution.

Disagreement over the meaning and compulsory nature of grouping became a major obstacle to implementation.

Constituent Assembly: composition and selection

The mission proposed a 389-member Constituent Assembly to frame the future constitution. The planned allocation was:

  • 292 representatives from the provinces of British India.
  • 4 representatives from Chief Commissioners' Provinces.
  • 93 representatives allocated to princely states.

The combined British Indian allocation was therefore 296 seats, and the total proposed strength was 389 seats.

Members representing British Indian provinces were to be chosen indirectly by members of provincial legislative assemblies, with General, Muslim and Sikh members separately electing their respective community's representatives by proportional representation with the single transferable vote. They were not elected directly by universal adult suffrage. Representation of princely states was to be settled through consultation.

Interim government and the plan's outcome

The mission also envisaged an interim government to administer British India while constitution-making proceeded. An interim government headed by Jawaharlal Nehru took office on 2 September 1946.

The Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946. However, the mission's intended united constitutional structure was not successfully established. Disagreements between the Congress and the Muslim League, especially concerning grouping and Pakistan, continued.

Ultimately, British India was partitioned in 1947, and India attained independence on 15 August 1947. The Cabinet Mission must therefore be distinguished from the later decision to partition British India.

Cabinet Mission compared with Cripps Mission

The Cripps Mission of 1942 offered a post-war constitutional settlement and allowed provinces to remain outside a proposed Union. The Cabinet Mission of 1946 attempted to begin constitution-making immediately and proposed a united India with a limited centre and provincial groups.

Prelims focus

  • Cabinet Mission members: Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps and A. V. Alexander.
  • Main Cabinet Mission statement: 16 May 1946.
  • Union subjects: foreign affairs, defence and communications, with necessary financial powers.
  • Provincial sections: A, B and C.
  • Proposed Constituent Assembly strength: 389 members.
  • Trap: The Cabinet Mission proposed a united India; it did not recommend the immediate creation of a sovereign Pakistan.

[British Cabinet Mission, Statement of 16 May 1946, paragraphs 11–19, reproduced in UK Parliament, House of Lords Debates, 16 May 1946, consulted 22 November 2026; NCERT, Indian Constitution at Work, Class 11, Chapter 1, Constitution: Why and How?, printed pp. 14–16.]

pictures.alt: The proposed Union holds specified powers; provinces retain other and residuary powers, while princely states retain powers not ceded.
pictures.caption: The plan proposed a limited Union, with extensive powers remaining with provinces and participating states.

pictures.alt: Planned seats: 292 provincial plus 4 Chief Commissioners’ seats make 296 for British India; adding 93 princely-state seats gives 389.
pictures.caption: The proposed Constituent Assembly had 389 seats, including 296 allocated to British India.

title: Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946: A United India, Provincial Groups and the Constituent Assembly

body:
Noakhali in the final phase of British rule

Noakhali was a district of eastern Bengal in undivided British India. The region is now in Bangladesh. In October 1946, it became the site of serious communal violence amid the growing political conflict over India's future.

The violence began on 10 October 1946. Hindu communities in Noakhali and neighbouring areas experienced attacks, killings, destruction of property and displacement. The events occurred during a wider period of Hindu–Muslim communal tension and insecurity in different parts of the subcontinent.

The incident was especially grave because it unfolded while British rule had not yet ended and negotiations concerning independence were still under way.

Gandhi's decision to visit the affected areas

Mahatma Gandhi regarded the restoration of communal peace as essential to India's future. Instead of concentrating solely on constitutional negotiations, he chose to visit the violence-affected villages.

Gandhi travelled to eastern Bengal and reached Chaumuhani on 7 November 1946. He subsequently stayed and worked in villages of Noakhali and neighbouring Tippera.

His objectives were to console those affected by violence, encourage displaced people to regain confidence, oppose communal hatred and rebuild relations between local communities.

The village-to-village peace mission

From 2 January 1947, Gandhi undertook an extensive walking peace mission through affected villages. His efforts included meetings, personal appeals and attempts to restore security and confidence among vulnerable residents.

The walking phase of the Noakhali mission continued until 1 March 1947. Gandhi then turned his attention to communal disturbances in Bihar.

The Noakhali mission was an example of Gandhi's attempt to address communal violence through direct contact with affected communities and non-violent peace efforts.

Relationship with the freedom struggle

The Noakhali events show that the final phase of the national movement involved 2 overlapping problems: ending British rule and preventing communal conflict. Constitutional negotiations could determine the formal transfer of political power, but they could not automatically resolve insecurity and hostility between communities.

Noakhali was not a constitutional commission, a British mission or an independence settlement. It was an episode of communal violence, followed by a major peace mission associated with Mahatma Gandhi.

The distinction between the date of the violence and the dates of Gandhi's visit is also important. The attacks began in October 1946; Gandhi reached the area in November 1946 and continued his peace work into 1947.

Prelims focus

  • Noakhali violence began: 10 October 1946.
  • Historical location: eastern Bengal, British India; now in Bangladesh.
  • Gandhi reached Chaumuhani: 7 November 1946.
  • Walking peace mission began: 2 January 1947.
  • Walking phase ended: 1 March 1947.
  • Trap: Noakhali violence occurred before independence, not after the Partition of August 1947.

[Gandhi Heritage Portal, Sabarmati Ashram Preservation and Memorial Trust, Noakhali, Bangladesh, sections Background and The Peace Mission, consulted 22 November 2026; Government of India, Gandhi-related historical chronology, entries for October 1946 and the Noakhali peace mission, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Villagers and peace volunteers discuss reconciliation beside thatched homes and baskets of relief supplies in rural eastern Bengal.
pictures.caption: Peace workers and villagers attempted to restore trust in violence-affected eastern Bengal.

pictures.alt: Timeline separates Noakhali violence and Gandhi’s arrival in 1946 from his walking peace mission and move to Bihar in 1947.
pictures.caption: Gandhi's peace mission followed the violence of October 1946 and continued into 1947.

title: Noakhali Violence and Gandhi's Peace Mission, 1946–1947

body:
How the events fit together

The developments from 1914 to 1947 form a connected sequence, but each had a different purpose. The Komagata Maru episode showed the unequal treatment of Indians under imperial rule. The Acts of 1919 and 1935 changed the machinery of government. The Simon Commission, Nehru Report and Round Table Conferences formed part of the debate over constitutional reform. The Cripps and Cabinet Missions attempted to resolve the political problem of transferring power. The INA trials and Noakhali violence shaped the atmosphere in which the final transfer occurred.

Chronology of the listed developments

YearDevelopmentCentral fact
1914Komagata MaruIndian passengers were denied entry to Canada; confrontation followed at Budge Budge.
1919Government of India ActIntroduced provincial dyarchy.
1927Simon Commission appointedAll-British commission chaired by Sir John Simon.
1928Simon Commission protestsOpposition to exclusion of Indian members.
1928Nehru ReportMotilal Nehru chaired the Indian constitutional committee.
1930–1932Round Table ConferencesThree constitutional conferences in London.
1935Government of India ActProvided provincial autonomy and proposed a federation.
1937Provincial electionsProvincial autonomy operated under the 1935 Act.
1942Cripps MissionPost-war dominion status proposed.
1945–1946INA trialsRed Fort court-martial and widespread nationalist response.
1946Cabinet MissionProposed a united constitutional structure and Constituent Assembly.
1946–1947NoakhaliCommunal violence followed by Gandhi's peace mission.
1947Independence and PartitionBritish India was partitioned and British rule ended.

Distinctions that prevent common mistakes

1919 and 1935: introduction versus abolition of provincial dyarchy

The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy in the provinces. The 1935 Act abolished provincial dyarchy and provided for provincial autonomy. The proposed central dyarchy under the 1935 Act did not operate because the federal scheme was not implemented.

Simon Commission and Nehru Report: British versus Indian initiative

The Simon Commission was appointed by the British government, had no Indian members and submitted its report in 1930. The Nehru Report was prepared by an Indian committee chaired by Motilal Nehru in 1928. It proposed dominion status and an Indian system of responsible government.

Dominion status and complete independence

Dominion status meant substantial internal self-government while retaining a constitutional relationship with the British Commonwealth and Crown. Complete independence, or Purna Swaraj, meant that India should be fully sovereign rather than remain politically dependent on Britain. The Nehru Report supported dominion status in 1928; the Congress adopted complete independence as its goal at Lahore in 1929.

Cripps Mission and Cabinet Mission: 1942 versus 1946

The Cripps Mission offered a post-war constitutional settlement and allowed provincial non-accession. The Cabinet Mission proposed immediate constitution-making arrangements for a united India, with only foreign affairs, defence and communications assigned to the Union.

INA trials and Noakhali: different events in the same final phase

The INA trials involved the prosecution of Indian military personnel and stirred nationalist sympathy. Noakhali involved communal violence in eastern Bengal and Gandhi's efforts to restore peace. Both belonged to the final phase of British rule, but neither was a constitutional commission or mission.

Final relationship between proposals and outcomes

British constitutional reform did not progress through a single uninterrupted plan. The 1919 Act introduced a restricted form of Indian participation; the Simon Commission examined its operation; Indian leaders responded with the Nehru Report; and the Round Table Conferences considered new arrangements. The 1935 Act introduced a new legal framework, but its federal proposal was not implemented.

During the Second World War, the Cripps Mission failed to produce agreement on an immediate transfer of authority. The Cabinet Mission later attempted to establish a united constitutional settlement, but disagreement over India's political future continued. The eventual outcome was independence accompanied by Partition in 1947.

Prelims focus

  • 1914: Komagata Maru.
  • 1919: provincial dyarchy introduced.
  • 1927–1928: Simon Commission appointed and opposed; Nehru Report prepared.
  • 1930–1935: Round Table Conferences followed by the Government of India Act, 1935.
  • 1942 and 1946: Cripps Mission and Cabinet Mission, respectively.
  • Trap: A constitutional proposal, a political conference and an enacted statute have different legal significance.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 120–126; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Chapter 2, Nationalism in India, printed pp. 62–65; NCERT, Indian Constitution at Work, Class 11, Chapter 1, Constitution: Why and How?, printed pp. 14–16; UK House of Lords Library, Lord Sinha of Raipur and the Government of India Act 1919, 2019, pp. 2–4; British Cabinet Mission Statement, 16 May 1946, UK Parliament, consulted 22 November 2026.]
